Description: S1, accounting for 11.69% of the SBS mutations, characterized by predominant C>T transitions. This signature showed high similarity to the SBS101 signature (cosine similarity=0.98) from the Signal database, which is prevalent in 68% of lymphoid cancers, and to SBSblood (cosine similarity=0.84), a recently identified SBS signature in normal human lymphocytes. While SBSblood exhibits additional T>C substitutions, both signatures share a predominant C>T pattern.

S2 is accounting for 9.51% of the SBS mutations, characterized by predominat  substitutions in TTT repeat regions and T>A mutations in TTW contexts. It is similar to COSMIC SBS41 (cosine similarity = 0.82) with unknown etilogy, and showed a high correlation with SHM rates in IGHV region genes (r=0.61) and displayed increased exposure in BL, FL, and DLBCL compared with CLL, MCL, and MM

S3, accounting for 9.44% of the SBS mutations, characterized by T>C mutations and displayed high similarity to Signal SBS26 (cosine similarity=0.94), which is associated with defective MMR. As expected, tumors harboring somatic mutations in MMR genes exhibited significantly higher this signature exposure than MMR-wild-type tumors

S4, accounting for 8.99% of the SBS mutations, is enriched in T>G transversions at the TW (W=A/T) motifs, showed strong similarity to Signal SBS9 (cosine similarity=0.98), which has been attributed to POLH-related mutations. Although POLH is reported to induce mutations at A:T base pairs in the TW or WA context during SHM, the mutation spectrum of S4 did not resemble the pattern observed in in vitro POLH experiments, which is characterized by enriched T>C mutations in the TW context.
S5, accounting for 8.81% of the SBS mutations, resembled COSMIC SBS1 (cosine similarity=0.98, clock-like endogenous processes)

S6, accounting for 8.67% of the SBS mutations, is characterized by C>A mutations with peaks at TCT and is similar to COSMIC SBS18 (cosine similarity=0.96), which has been linked to BER deficiency. S6 showed significantly higher exposure in BER-mutated tumors than in BER-unmutated tumors (see manuscript), suggesting that this signature may result from BER deficiency.

S7, accounting for 8.34% of the SBS mutations, is dominated by T>G transversions substitutions in NTT regions and T>C transitions substitutions in CTT regions, closely resembled Signal SBS17 (cosine similarity=0.99), which has been reported in multiple cancer types and normal memory B cells. Although the etiology of SBS17 remains unclear, it has been linked to oxidative damage in nucleoid pools or microenvironmental exposure such as gastric acid in resident tissues. This signature was nearly absent in U-CLL and cMCL but was comparable to that in the other subtypes, suggesting a potential association with GC-related microenvironmental factors.

S8, accounting for 8.28% of the SBS mutations, is characterized by elevated C>A, T>A, and C>T mutations, closely resembled SBS8 (cosine similarity=0.95), tentatively proposed to HR or NER deficiencies in the COSMIC. This signature exposure was significantly higher in NER-mutated tumors compared to NER-unmutated tumors, but only slightly increased in HR-mutated tumors than in HR-unmutated tumors, indicating a stronger association with NER deficiency.

S9, accounting for 6.91% of the SBS mutations, characterized by T>C mutations at TW motifs, exhibited features consistent with POLH-mediated mutagenesis. It showed similar mutational pattern with several reported POLH-associated signatures, including COSMIC SBS85 and experimentally derived POLH-induced mutational signature, moderate similarity to these signatures (cosine similarity=0.81-0.85), and strong correlation with experimentally derived POLH-induced mutations, supporting its association with POLH activity (check more in paper)
S10, accounting for 5.83% of the SBS mutations, resembled Signal SBS5 (cosine similarity=0.85, clock-like endogenous processes)

S11, accounting for 5.32% of the SBS mutations, is dominated by C>G transversions and a peak at TCT>TGT, closely resembled SBS3 (cosine similarity=0.91), which has been associated with HR deficiency, including BRCA1/2 mutations in breast cancers. Tis exposure was significantly higher in HR-mutated tumors, and showed no obvious variation across B-cell subtypes.

S12 is accounting for 4.19% of the SBS mutations, is dominated by T>G in the GTT context and of T>C mutations in the GTC/TTC context. It is similar to COSMIC SBS106 (cosine similarity = 0.85) with unknown etilogy. Its exposure was less prevalent in the poor-prognosis subtypes (U-CLL, cMCL, and ABC-DLBCL) than in their more favorable counterparts
S13, accounting for 4.3% of the SBS mutations, is dominated by C>T at NCG trinucleotides, resembled SBS2 (q=0.97), suggesting its association with the activities of APOBEC family members.

D1, accounting for 30.04% of the DBS mutations, is characterized by mutations in TT, AT, and TA, consistent with POLH-mediated mutagenesis in the TW or WA context (W=A/T). D1 exhibited high similarity to Signal DBS22 (q=0.82), a signature reported to be largely restricted in lymphoid cancer. , D1 exposure correlated strongly with the POLH-associated SBS signatures S9 and S4.
D2, accounting for 24.27% of the DBS mutations, is characterized by TG>CA, TC>CT, and CT>TC mutations, and  shows no strong similarity with Signal_SBS21 (cosine similarity=0.8, defective MMR).

D3, accounting for 24.08% of the DBS mutations, shows a dominant CC>AA mutation pattern and closely resembled Signal DBS13 (cosine similarity=0.93), a signature with unknown etiology that reported in multiple solid cancers.

D4, accounting for 21.6% of the DBS mutations (cosine similarity=0.93), is characterized by CC>TT and GC>AN mutations and resembles Signal DBS32 (cosine similarity=0.84) with unknown etiology, and COSMIC DBS11 (cosine similarity=0.84) with proposed APOBEC activity.

ID1, accounting for 49.1% of the indels, closely resembled COSMIC ID2 (cosine similarity=0.98) and was characterized by deletions of thymine at long (>5) mononucleotide repeats, a pattern typically associated with defective MMR (see manuscript). Its exposure was higher in MMR-mutated tumors than in MMR-unmutated tumors and elevated in GC tumors.

ID2 accounted for 34.24% of the indels and was characterized by both deletions and insertions of thymine at long (>5) repeats. This signature showed a high cosine similarity with COSMIC ID1 (cosine similarity=0.9), which has been linked to aging in non-hypermutated samples and is elevated in cancers with MMR-deficiency. The exposure of ID2 was also significantly higher in MMR-mutated tumors than in MMR-unmutated tumors.

ID3, accounted for 16.35% of the indels, characterized by a >1 bp deletion involving a single repeat unit and 1 bp deletions of thymine and cytidine within homopolymers of length ³2, represents a novel indel signature that does not resemble any previously reported signatures and could not be further decomposed

K1 was characterized predominantly by C>T mutations and was highly enriched in the well-known AID motif WRCY (W=A/T, R=A/G, Y=C/T). K1 was predominantly enriched in IGH S regions, and in the IGHD-Ecosine similarity, IGLJ-C, and TSS-proximal regions of ABC-DLBCL and BL.

K2 was characterized by T>N mutations in the NTW (N=A/T/C/G, W=A/T) context, was enriched for the POLH motif TW, and showed a high similarity to the mutation pattern induced by POLH.K2 was more prevalent in IGK and distal TSS regions.
